h2: Pool Equipment Seminyak – Pumps, Filters & Chlorinators
intro: Pool Equipment Seminyak repairs and installations cover everything from silent-running pumps to salt chlorinators that keep villa water safe for guests. In a dense area where plots sit shoulder-to-shoulder and many pools were installed fifteen to twenty-five years ago, small failures can escalate fast. We handle the full range – pumps, sand and cartridge filters, multiport valves, underwater lighting, and auto-fill systems.

sections.h3: Why Older Villas Need More Attention
sections.text: In Petitenget and Oberoi, many villa plots are narrow with shared retaining walls, which means the pump room is often a cramped corner behind a kitchen or under a staircase. Fifteen-to-twenty-five-year-old pipework corrodes from the inside, and a single cracked union can flood that tight space before anyone notices. We work around those constraints – routing new lines through existing chases, swapping worn multiport valves without tearing up tile, and replacing tired pumps where headroom barely allows it.

sections.h3: Common Pool Failures Between Guest Check-ins
sections.text: High-occupancy rentals across Seminyak's lanes mean the pool takes a beating between check-ins. A pump that stops priming on a Tuesday morning, a cartridge filter clogged with sunscreen residue, or a salt chlorinator throwing an error code while guests are still in the water – these need sorting fast so the next booking isn't affected. Noisy bearings, leaking auto-fill solenoids, and flickering underwater lights are the jobs we see most often in this rhythm.

sections.h3: What to Send Before Booking a Visit
sections.text: Before we schedule anything, send a few clear photos on WhatsApp: the pump nameplate or model sticker, the filter housing (sand or cartridge), any visible leaks or error displays on the chlorinator, and a short note describing what you hear or see. If the pool light is out, a photo of the junction box helps. Once we have that, we can tell you whether it's a parts swap or a full replacement, and give you a quote based on the actual job.

sections.h3: Keeping Your Pool Running Through Wet Season
sections.text: Heavy rain in Drupadi and surrounding lanes sends water into low-lying pump rooms and overloads septic lines, which can back up into your filter housing. A few habits save headaches: backwash the sand filter every two to three weeks even if pressure looks fine, check the auto-fill float for algae buildup monthly, and wipe down chlorinator cells after each cleaning cycle. If a lane floods and your pump room gets wet, switch off the breaker before touching anything and send us a photo – corrosion starts within hours.

faq.q: How do I know if my sand filter needs new media?
faq.a: If backwashing no longer brings pressure back to normal or you see fine grit in the return jets, the sand is likely broken down. Send a photo of the gauge reading on WhatsApp and we'll confirm.

faq.q: Can you replace just the multiport valve without draining the pool?
faq.a: In most cases yes – we isolate the line, swap the valve body, and re-seal the unions while water stays in the basin. Access to the pump room determines how straightforward it is.

faq.q: What should I check after a street flood hits my lane?
faq.a: Look for standing water around the pump motor and chlorinator cabinet; if either got wet, cut power at the breaker and message us a photo before switching anything back on.
